s01.text: Most people assume a USB-C charging cable is just a passive bundle of copper wires inside plastic.

s02.text: In reality, high-power USB-C cables contain an active computer inside the plug: an electronic marker chip.

s03.text: Standard copper wires can safely carry three amps of current. Forcing five amps through thin wire produces violent resistive heating and melts the insulation.

s04.text: To prevent electrical fires, the E-Marker chip negotiates directly with your charger using high-frequency packets on the Configuration Channel pin.

s05.text: It broadcasts its vendor identity, wire gauge rating, and maximum voltage: authorizing up to two hundred and forty watts under Extended Power Range.

s06.text: If your charger doesn't detect that digital signature, it hard-caps electrical current to sixty watts, protecting cheap cables from burning.

s07.text: USB-C didn't just unify our connectors: it turned dumb copper wire into a communicating computer on your desk.
